title: A form of refined Roth's theorem and its application to the $abc$-conjecture

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper says, “we will prove Conjecture 1.2 for algebraic integers,” but Conjecture 1.2, Eq. (9), has truncated counting functions \(\overline N\). Theorem 1.4 instead asserts Eq. (11) with the ordinary, multiplicity-counting functions \(N(x,a_j)\). Since \(\overline N(x,a)\le N(x,a)\), Eq. (11) is a strictly weaker statement and does not prove the claimed restricted case of Conjecture 1.2.

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 2.1 proof, construction of \(x'\) after Eq. (19), and the subsequent Remark
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorem 2.1 asserts that there exist a field \(K\) and a single element \(x'\in K\) such that the inequality holds for all but finitely many \(x\in\kappa\). But the purported construction of \(x'\) in the Remark explicitly starts from factorizations of \((x)\) and \((x-a_j)\), defines \(a_0\), \(a_\infty\), \(x_0\), and \(x_\infty\) from their prime factors and exponents, and then sets \(x'=x_0/x_\infty\). Thus \(x'\) varies with \(x\). This does not establish the existence of one fixed \(x'\) required by Theorem 2.1, and subsequent bounds treating \(x'\) as fixed cannot yield the stated uniform conclusion.

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 2.1 proof, transition from Eq. (16) to Eq. (19)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Eq. (16) has ordinary counting functions \(N(x,\infty)+\sum_jN(x,a_j)\) and the correction term \(-N_{x'}(x)\). Eq. (19) suddenly replaces every \(N\) by \(\overline N\): “which implies by (16) that ... \(\overline N(x,\infty)+\sum \overline N(x,a_j)\) ...”. No equality or inequality proving this replacement is supplied. The definitions of \(a_0,a_\infty\) that might have been intended to control multiplicities are absent from the main proof and, in the later Remark, depend on \(x\), so they cannot justify the asserted fixed-\(x'\) result.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 1.4, paragraph invoking Dirichlet's unit theorem
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof claims that Dirichlet's unit theorem gives a constant \(c(\kappa)\) such that \(|y|_v\le c(\kappa)|y|_w\) for every algebraic integer \(y\) and all Archimedean places \(v,w\). This is false. In a number field with a non-torsion unit \(u\), the ratios \(|u^n|_v/|u^n|_w\) are unbounded as \(n\to\infty\) for suitable Archimedean places. Dirichlet's theorem describes the unit lattice; it does not uniformly bound ratios of all Archimedean conjugates. Consequently the asserted conclusion \(m(y,0)=O(1)\), which is essential for removing the proximity term, is unsupported and generally false.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 1.4, use of \(K\) versus \(\kappa\)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorem 2.1 constructs \(x'\in K\), so \(y=1/(x'Q(x))\) lies in \(K\), not generally in \(\kappa\). Nevertheless the proof of Theorem 1.4 invokes \(M_\kappa^\infty\), a constant \(c(\kappa)\), and the previously defined proximity/counting functions over \(\kappa\) when discussing \(y\). The proof earlier changed the relevant field to \(K\) for \(Q(x)\), but does not consistently redefine heights, places, \(S\), or normalizations for \(y\in K\). This field mismatch invalidates the displayed argument even apart from the false unit-theorem assertion.

predicted_errors.error_location: Derivation of Eq. (21) from Theorem 1.5 / Eq. (12)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorem 1.5 gives \(h(x)\le N(x,\infty)+N(x,a_1)+N(x,a_2)+O(1)\), with untruncated \(N\). The paper then says that applying Eq. (12) to \(x=a/c\) gives Eq. (21), whose right-hand side consists of \(\overline N(a/c,0),\overline N(a/c,-1),\overline N(a/c,\infty)\). This replacement is invalid. The condition that one of \(a,b,c\), namely \(c\), is squarefree can make the denominator contribution truncated, but it does not make the numerator factors \(a\) and \(b\) squarefree or imply \(N(a/c,0)=\overline N(a/c,0)\) and \(N(a/c,-1)=\overline N(a/c,-1)\). Hence the claimed abc consequence does not follow.

predicted_errors.error_location: Final proof of Theorem 1.6, immediately after Eq. (21)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The theorem and preceding discussion assume \(a+b=c\). The proof then states, “Since \(a+b+c=0\),” and identifies the \(-1\)-term for \(x=a/c\) with the prime divisors of \(b\). Under \(a+b=c\), however, \(a/c-1=-b/c\), so the relevant target is \(1\), not \(-1\). The identity \(a+b+c=0\) would require replacing one variable by its negative, but no such change of variables is stated. Thus the displayed identifications and the application of Eq. (12) are inconsistent with the theorem's stated equation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorems 1.4 and 1.5 and definitions of \(N(x,a)\), \(\overline N(x,a)\)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorems 1.4 and 1.5 state \(a_j\in\overline\kappa\), while the preceding definitions of \(\chi_v(x,a)\), \(N(x,a)\), and the ideal/valuation formulae require \(x-a\in\kappa\) and are only defined for \(a\in\kappa\). Theorem 2.1 itself restricts to \(a_1,\ldots,a_q\in\kappa\). Although the text says “without loss of generality” one may assume the \(a_j\) lie in \(\kappa\), it gives no valid reformulation over an extension field, no extensions of the places for the counting functions, and no accounting for the changed normalization. As written, the theorem statements are not even defined for their claimed coefficients.

After deriving \(|Q(x)|_v>\rho_v/(2|x-a_j|_v)\), the proof writes \(\log^+\|Q(x)\|_v>\log^+(1/\|x-a_j\|_v)-n_v\log(2/\rho_v)\). This is not valid when \(\rho_v>2\): the right side can be positive even if \(1/\|x-a_j\|_v<1\), while the lower bound \(\rho_v/(2|x-a_j|_v)\) need not force \(\|Q(x)\|_v>1\). A universally valid coarse estimate needs a nonnegative error such as \(n_v\log^+(2/\rho_v)\), with appropriate case handling. The stated inequality and the resulting constant \(C_S\) therefore are not justified as written.

The paper repeatedly relies on references [1], [2], [3], and [4], including “see [3], Theorem 6.14,” “see [3], p. 358,” “Theorem 2.32,” and “Theorem 2.36 and Lemma 4.3 in [3].” However, the supplied bibliography begins at [5] and contains only [5] through [15]. These sources are absent, so the central attributions and quoted theorem numbering cannot be checked and the bibliography is incomplete.
